note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's land is covered by forest?
questions.whyCorrect: 31% — about 4.1 billion hectares. Roughly a third of all land, and shrinking by 10 million hectares a year.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — forests still cover about a third of land.
questions.action: Find out what share of your country is forested.

questions.prompt: How much forest did the world lose between 2000 and 2020?
questions.whyCorrect: 100 million hectares — an area roughly the size of Egypt, cleared in twenty years.
questions.action: Find a country about 100 million hectares in size.

questions.prompt: How much forest is lost every year now?
questions.whyCorrect: About 10 million hectares a year, down from 12 million in 2010–2015. Slowing, but still an area the size of Iceland annually.
questions.action: Ask what replaces a cleared forest.

questions.prompt: The rate of deforestation between 2010-2015 and 2015-2020:
questions.whyCorrect: Fell from 12 to 10 million hectares a year — genuine progress, though at that rate it would take 25 years just to reach zero.
questions.action: Ask what would need to happen to reach zero deforestation.

questions.prompt: At current rates, how long would it take to halt deforestation entirely?
questions.whyCorrect: About 25 years at the current rate of improvement — far beyond the 2030 deadline the world set itself.
whyWrong: 10 million hectares are still lost yearly.
Progress is far slower than this.
questions.action: Count forward 25 years from today.

questions.prompt: Brazil cut deforestation in the Legal Amazon in 2023 by:
questions.whyCorrect: 50% in a single year, compared with 2022 — proof that deforestation responds fast to political decisions and enforcement.
questions.action: Ask what Brazil changed to halve deforestation.

questions.prompt: Indonesia reduced deforestation by how much?
questions.whyCorrect: 14% between 2021–22 and 2020–21 — smaller than Brazil's 50%, but part of the same encouraging pattern.
questions.action: Look up why Indonesian forests are cleared.

questions.prompt: How much CO2 did wildfires release in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: 6,687 megatons — comparable to the annual emissions of the world's largest economies, from fires alone.
questions.action: Compare wildfire emissions with your country's total.

questions.prompt: How much land degrades every year, at minimum?
questions.whyCorrect: At least 100 million hectares a year — ten times the rate of deforestation, and it affects 3.2 billion people.
questions.action: Ask what turns good farmland into degraded land.

questions.prompt: How many people are affected by land degradation?
questions.whyCorrect: 3.2 billion — around 40% of humanity live on or depend on degrading land, mostly farmers and herders.
questions.action: Ask what a farmer does when soil stops producing.

questions.prompt: The share of land that is degraded rose from 11.3% in 2015 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 15.5% by 2019 — a rise of over four percentage points in four years, one of the fastest-worsening SDG indicators.
questions.action: Ask what 15.5% of the world's land area amounts to.

questions.prompt: How much land needs restoring by 2030?
questions.whyCorrect: About 1.5 billion hectares — roughly the size of Russia. It's the largest restoration commitment humanity has ever made.
whyWrong: Degraded land covers 15.5% of the planet's surface.
questions.action: Find a country about 1.5 billion hectares in size.

questions.prompt: Land restoration needs how much money per day between 2025 and 2030?
questions.whyCorrect: $1 billion a day. Current funding is $66 billion a year — about 18% of what's needed.
questions.action: Multiply $1 billion by 365 days.

questions.prompt: Land restoration funding currently covers what share of the need?
questions.whyCorrect: 18% — $66 billion a year against a need of roughly $365 billion. The gap, not the ambition, is the obstacle.
questions.action: Ask why restoring land is hard to fund.

questions.prompt: How many species are threatened with extinction?
questions.whyCorrect: Over 47,000 assessed species — and most species on Earth have never been assessed at all.
questions.action: Look up one threatened species in your country.

questions.prompt: The Red List Index of species survival has declined how much since 1993?
questions.whyCorrect: 12% — a steady, unbroken decline over three decades. The index measures how close assessed species are to extinction overall.
questions.action: Look up what the IUCN Red List categories mean.

questions.prompt: What share of assessed tree species face extinction?
questions.whyCorrect: 38% of 47,282 assessed tree species — more than a third of the world's tree types are at risk, not just forest area.
questions.action: Ask how many tree species grow near you.

questions.prompt: What share of freshwater species are threatened?
questions.whyCorrect: 25% — a quarter of all freshwater species. Rivers and lakes hold a huge share of biodiversity in a tiny share of the world's water.
whyWrong: Too high, though the real figure is severe.
questions.action: Ask what lives in the nearest river to you.

questions.prompt: What share of land and inland water is protected?
questions.whyCorrect: 17.6% — the 2020 target was met on land, unlike the ocean's 8.4%. Land conservation is well ahead of marine.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — the land target was met.
questions.action: Find the nearest national park to your home.

questions.prompt: What share of key biodiversity areas fall within protected areas?
questions.whyCorrect: 68% — protection is well targeted at the places that matter most, though a third of critical sites still lack it.
questions.action: Ask how scientists identify a key biodiversity area.

questions.prompt: Mean protection of key biodiversity areas rose from 25% in 2000 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 44% by 2024 — nearly doubled in a quarter century. One of the clearest conservation successes on record.
questions.action: Ask what makes protection expand over decades.

questions.prompt: How much biodiversity development finance flowed in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: $11.9 billion, up from $9.5 billion in 2015 — but only 7% of all development finance goes to biodiversity.
questions.action: Compare $11.9 billion with the $1 billion needed daily for land restoration.

questions.prompt: Funding where biodiversity is the PRINCIPAL objective went from $4.6 billion in 2015 to:
questions.whyCorrect: It FELL to $3.8 billion. Total biodiversity finance rose, but money dedicated primarily to nature actually declined.
whyWrong: Principal-objective funding fell rather than rose.
questions.action: Ask the difference between a principal and a secondary objective.

questions.prompt: Biodiversity is what share of all development finance?
questions.whyCorrect: 7% — nature gets a small slice, even though land degradation affects 3.2 billion people directly.
questions.action: Ask what the other 93% of development finance funds.

questions.prompt: Private biodiversity finance grew from $748 million in 2021 to about:
questions.whyCorrect: Roughly $4 billion by 2023 — more than five times in two years. Private money is the fastest-growing part of nature finance.
questions.action: Ask why a company would fund conservation.

questions.prompt: How much roundwood does the world harvest each year?
questions.whyCorrect: 4 billion cubic metres — for construction, paper, and firewood, which is still the main cooking fuel for billions.
questions.action: List five wooden or paper items around you.

questions.prompt: Land degradation rising from 11.3% to 15.5% in four years means:
options: An area larger than many continents was degraded in that short window
questions.whyCorrect: A 4.2-point rise across the world's land surface is an enormous absolute area — degrading faster than restoration can keep up.
whyWrong: It is one of the fastest-moving negative indicators.
questions.action: Ask how much land 4.2% of the Earth's surface is.

questions.prompt: Land degradation means:
options: Soil, vegetation and water systems losing their ability to support life and crops
questions.whyCorrect: Erosion, salt build-up, nutrient loss and drying all reduce what land can produce — which is why it affects 3.2 billion people's livelihoods.
whyWrong: Protection is the opposite of degradation.
It's an ecological process, not a market one.
questions.action: Look at bare soil after heavy rain and see where it goes.

questions.prompt: 38% of tree species facing extinction matters because:
options: Losing tree diversity weakens forests' resilience to pests, drought and fire
questions.whyCorrect: A forest of one species falls to one disease. Diversity is what lets forests survive shocks — which is why species loss matters beyond area loss.
whyWrong: 47,282 species were assessed, common ones included.
A mature forest takes decades to centuries to replace.
questions.action: Look up a tree species wiped out by a single disease.

questions.prompt: Brazil halved Amazon deforestation in one year. The clearest lesson is:
options: Enforcement and political will can change the rate very quickly
questions.whyCorrect: Forests aren't lost by natural forces — they're cleared by decisions. Change the decisions and the satellite data changes within months.
whyWrong: Brazil cut it 50% in a single year.
Satellite monitoring makes deforestation highly measurable.
questions.action: Look up how satellites detect deforestation.

questions.prompt: Land protection is 17.6% while ocean protection is 8.4%. This shows:
options: Land conservation is roughly twice as far along as marine
questions.whyCorrect: Land is easier to fence, patrol and legislate. The ocean's vastness and shared ownership make protection far harder.
whyWrong: Ocean protection is less than half the land figure.
The gap is over nine percentage points.
questions.action: Ask who owns the middle of the ocean.

questions.prompt: Key biodiversity area protection nearly doubled from 25% to 44%. That happened over:
questions.whyCorrect: From 2000 to 2024 — showing that sustained conservation policy compounds into large gains over decades.
whyWrong: Modern protected area systems are much younger.
Far too short a period for such change.
questions.action: Ask what your country protected in the last twenty years.

questions.prompt: Wildfires emitting 6,687 megatons of CO2 creates a feedback loop because:
options: Warming causes more fires, and fires release carbon that causes more warming
questions.whyCorrect: Hotter, drier conditions make fires more likely; each fire adds carbon that makes conditions hotter still. Feedback loops are what make climate change accelerate.
whyWrong: Fires release large amounts of stored carbon.
Fire and climate are tightly linked.
questions.action: Look up how fire seasons have changed where you live.

questions.prompt: Total biodiversity finance rose but principal-objective finance fell. This suggests:
options: More money mentions nature, while less is dedicated primarily to it
questions.whyCorrect: $9.5bn to $11.9bn total, but $4.6bn to $3.8bn for projects where nature is the main aim — headline growth hides a decline in dedicated funding.
whyWrong: Both figures moved, in opposite directions.
questions.action: Ask why headline totals can hide a decline.

questions.prompt: 1.5 billion hectares of restoration by 2030 requires restoring roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: Around 300 million hectares a year over five years — thirty times the rate at which forests are currently being lost.
questions.action: Divide 1.5 billion by five years.

questions.prompt: 25% of freshwater species being threatened is notable because freshwater covers:
options: Under 1% of Earth's surface, yet holds a huge share of biodiversity
questions.whyCorrect: Rivers and lakes are a tiny fraction of the planet but home to an outsized share of species — which makes them extraordinarily vulnerable.
whyWrong: Oceans cover most of the surface; freshwater is a sliver.
Freshwater ecosystems are extensive despite small area.
questions.action: Ask what happens to a river species when the river is dammed.

questions.prompt: The Red List Index falling 12% since 1993 means:
options: Assessed species are moving steadily closer to extinction overall
questions.whyCorrect: The index tracks aggregate extinction risk across assessed species. A steady 12% decline means the overall trend is toward loss, not recovery.
whyWrong: It measures risk, not completed extinctions.
The index has declined without interruption.
questions.action: Look up a species that moved to a lower risk category.

questions.prompt: Forests covering 4.1 billion hectares means the average person has about:
questions.whyCorrect: Roughly half a hectare each — 4.1 billion hectares divided among 8 billion people, and falling every year.
questions.action: Divide 4.1 billion by 8 billion.

questions.prompt: Land degrades at 100 million hectares a year while forest is lost at 10 million. This means:
options: Degradation is ten times faster than deforestation
questions.whyCorrect: Degradation is the larger and less visible crisis — land doesn't have to be cleared to stop producing food.
whyWrong: Degradation is ten times the rate.
The rates differ by a factor of ten.
questions.action: Ask why degradation gets less attention than deforestation.

questions.prompt: 68% of key biodiversity areas are protected, but that leaves:
options: Nearly a third of the world's most critical habitats unprotected
questions.whyCorrect: 32% of the sites scientists identify as most important for species survival still have no formal protection at all.
questions.action: Ask what stops a critical site being protected.

questions.prompt: Deforestation slowing from 12 to 10 million hectares a year is:
options: Real progress, but nowhere near the pace needed for 2030
questions.whyCorrect: A 17% improvement is genuine — but at that rate it takes 25 years to reach zero, long past the 2030 deadline.
whyWrong: 10 million hectares are still lost yearly.
questions.action: Ask what 'progress but not enough' means for a deadline.

questions.prompt: Why does forest loss matter for climate as well as wildlife?
options: Forests store carbon; clearing them releases it and removes future absorption
questions.whyCorrect: A cleared forest gives up its stored carbon and stops absorbing more — a double loss. Wildfires alone released 6,687 megatons in 2023.
whyWrong: Forests are among the largest carbon stores on land.
Standing forests absorb carbon on balance.
questions.action: Look up how much carbon one mature tree stores.

questions.prompt: $66 billion a year against a $365 billion need means restoration is funded at:
questions.whyCorrect: About 18% — the plans exist and the science exists; the money is roughly a fifth of what the plans require.
questions.action: Divide 66 by 365.

questions.prompt: Which Goal 15 indicator is clearly improving?
options: Protection of key biodiversity areas, from 25% to 44%
questions.whyCorrect: Protection nearly doubled since 2000. Degradation rose from 11.3% to 15.5% and the Red List Index fell 12% — both worsening.
whyWrong: The Red List Index has declined 12%.
questions.action: Find one protected area created near you in your lifetime.

questions.prompt: 47,000 threatened species is likely an undercount because:
options: Most species on Earth have never been formally assessed
questions.whyCorrect: Assessment requires years of fieldwork per species. Insects, fungi and deep-sea life are barely covered, so the real figure is far higher.
whyWrong: Red List assessments are conservative by design.
Millions of species exist; most are unassessed.
questions.action: Look up how many species scientists estimate exist.

questions.prompt: Private biodiversity finance rising from $748 million to $4 billion suggests:
options: Companies increasingly see nature loss as a business risk
questions.whyCorrect: Supply chains depend on soil, water and pollinators. As those degrade, companies start paying to protect what their business rests on.
whyWrong: Restoration costs are rising, not falling.
questions.action: Name a product that depends on pollinating insects.

questions.prompt: 3.2 billion people affected by land degradation are mostly:
options: Farmers, herders and rural communities who depend directly on the land
questions.whyCorrect: When soil fails, the people who eat from it lose food and income first — which is why land degradation drives migration and conflict.
whyWrong: Urban workers feel it through food prices, not directly.
questions.action: Ask where a farming family goes when the land fails.

questions.prompt: Forests cover 31% of land while 17.6% of land is protected. This means:
options: Most forest lies outside protected areas
questions.whyCorrect: Protected areas include deserts, grasslands and mountains as well as forest — so most of the world's forest has no formal protection.
whyWrong: Protected area is well below forest area.
questions.action: Check whether the nearest woodland to you is protected.

questions.prompt: Restoring 1.5 billion hectares would mainly deliver:
options: Food security, carbon storage and habitat, all at once
questions.whyCorrect: Restored land feeds people, stores carbon and shelters species simultaneously — which is why it appears in the climate, hunger and biodiversity goals alike.
whyWrong: Restoration produces measurable gains across several goals.
The benefits are economic and ecological, not aesthetic.
questions.action: Find a restoration project near you and see what it produced.

questions.prompt: The most under-recognised Goal 15 fact is:
options: Land degrades ten times faster than forests are cleared, affecting 3.2 billion people
questions.whyCorrect: Deforestation gets the headlines; degradation is ten times larger, quieter, and hits the livelihoods of nearly half of humanity.
whyWrong: Protection is the success story, not the hidden crisis.
questions.action: Look for signs of soil erosion near where you live.
